Executive Summary

This portfolio has recovered $370.62 of $60,793.68 placed — a liquidation rate of 0.61%. Two accounts have resolved: Pierce, Tracy ($195.10), Tantra Brew House ($175.52). The remaining $77,729.78 open balance is spread across 84 accounts averaging $925.35.

Across 86 placed accounts, Southwest Recovery Services has logged 11,597 individual collection actions since 04/20/2023: 5,024 outbound call attempts (3,028 ending in a voicemail or delivered message), 5,839 emails, 517 collection letters, 84 validation notices, 74 skip-trace actions, 47 text messages and 8 inbound contacts.

The open balance is $18,606.72 higher than the amount originally placed on those accounts because of balance updates recorded after placement. Individual account activity, the numbers on file and the complete note log are available by expanding any account in the Account Detail section below.

Why Balances Remain Unpaid

We reviewed the 302 documents you uploaded to the portal (invoices, placement files and summaries), the numbers on file, and the complete trail of 17,911 account notes. No single factor explains the result. These are all of the reasons we can document, grouped so you can see which are inside our control, which are inside MI-BOX’s, and which are the debtors’.

Outcome to date: $370.62 recovered of $60,793.68 placed (0.61%), on two accounts. A conversation with the debtor is documented on 11 of the 86 accounts.
1. Inside our control
  • Accounts were run by automation, not worked by people. Of 17,911 notes, 136 were written by a person. 20 accounts have no human note at all. The typical last human note is about 93 days old, and 25 of the 66 accounts that have one are over 180 days old. 64 accounts are still in “New Business.”
  • Volume without results. 5,024 call attempts (4,437 AI, 404 dialer, 183 collector) and 5,839 emails produced 8 inbound contacts.
  • We kept using contact details you told us were bad. Your placement files flag bounced emails on 23 of 180 rows and delivery-site addresses on 13. Contact continued, including about 286 emails to seven flagged addresses after the warning.
  • We never asked you for what we needed. The messages we sent were thank-you notes and six missing-field notices. None asked about signed agreements, who signed, the card on file or the containers.
  • Your documents were hard to use. Your uploads sit on your client account, not on each debtor, and each monthly invoice became its own account (35 accounts for 13 debtors, each with its own letters and emails). Our acknowledgment of your uploads took a median of three days; 159 of 301 took longer.
2. Inside MI-BOX’s control
  • Thin placement files. One phone number per placement (88% in the “Other Phone” field), no date of birth or SSN on any of the 180 placement rows, and an account number on 3%.
  • Late placement. Accounts reached us a median of about 140 days after the invoice was due, and 43 of the 111 invoices we have were over 180 days old. Industry benchmark data puts the chance of collecting at about 69% at three months past due, 51% at six, 21% at twelve and 9% at twenty-four. These are benchmarks, not a promise.
  • Few documents. We have one executed agreement for 63 debtors, and a written summary for 5 of them.
  • Declined cards. 39 of the 111 invoices we have note a card on file that was declined or could not be charged.
3. The debtors’
  • Not responding. 3,028 call attempts ended in a voicemail or delivered message. Only 8 inbound contacts were recorded in more than three years.
  • Disputes we could not answer. Some debtors say they never signed or contest damage charges. Without the signed agreement and evidence we could not resolve them.
  • Contact stopped. Two accounts are in Cease and Desist at the debtor’s request and one was removed at your direction.

Signed Agreements vs. Invoices

We received invoices for 24 of your 63 debtors (111 invoices totaling $37,577.90), your placement spreadsheet for every account, and one executed agreement (a storage agreement signed in 2019). The agreement sets late fees at $15 after 10 days and $25 after 30 days, and a billing sheet describes a further $25 for each month past due.

Invoice typeInvoicesAmountWhat the invoices show
Monthly container rent (recurring)94$27,413.95Late-fee lines total $7,985.00 (29% of these invoices). On 35 of them the late fees exceed half of the base rent charge.
One-time invoices (repairs, pickups, cleaning, damage)17$10,163.95No photos or work orders came with them. Three of the monthly invoices also carry a pickup or damage line ($929.46).
This explains some of the resistance we meet. Debtors may pay or accept the rent and contest the late fees and damage charges, and we cannot answer a dispute without the signed agreement and evidence. Separating rent, late fees and damages on each invoice makes every balance easier to explain.

What we need from MI-BOX to succeed, and why each one matters
We needWhy it matters to collecting
Signed agreement for each debtor, and who signed itIt is the proof of what the debtor agreed to: rent, late charges, the card authorization. Without it, one dispute can stop an account. On business accounts it also shows who signed and whether a person, not just the company, is responsible.
Second phone, alternate contact, working emailWe received one phone number per debtor. When it fails, we have no other way to reach them. 23 of your 180 placement rows say the email bounces.
Billing address, apart from the delivery addressLetters and notices sent to a job site or delivery location never reach the debtor. Your files flagged 13. We cannot locate or confirm who we are dealing with from a delivery address.
Card on file: declined or not, and a retryThe agreement lets MI-BOX charge the card after 30 days late. It is the fastest, cheapest recovery. If it fails, it tells us what to expect. 39 of the invoices we have show a declined card.
Container status: on site, picked up, dateShows whether MI-BOX still holds the container and its contents, which is real leverage, and whether rent is still adding to the balance.
Damage evidence: photos, work orders, repair costDamage charges are the first thing debtors dispute ($10,163.95 on 17 one-time invoices). Evidence is what resolves a dispute and lets us keep working the account.
Payments received directly, and payment plansSo we never contact someone who has paid or is on a plan, and the balance we quote is right.
Short summary on your 15 largest accountsThe history that does not fit in a file: promises, conversations, disputes. A person can start at the right place, not from zero. We have a summary for only 5 of your 63 debtors.
One monthly file per debtor, with a ledgerSeparates rent, late fees and damages so a balance can be explained and defended, and puts one debtor on one account.
Identifiers, whatever you have: date of birth, last four of driver’s license or SSN, business tax ID, employerThese let us confirm we have the right person, find them when they move, check bankruptcy, deceased and military status before we contact anyone, and match the account for credit reporting. None of the 180 placement rows had a date of birth or SSN. Your agreement uses the last four of the driver’s license as the access PIN, so you may already have it.
Why speed matters. Each month between the due date and placement lowers the chance of collecting, and missing contact details and identifiers make every one of those months worse. A standing weekly placement file of everything unpaid at 30 days would put accounts in front of us while they are most collectable.
What we will do if you give us the chance
WhenWhat happens
Week 1Stop contact on addresses and emails marked bad. A named collector reviews every account over $1,000. Combine accounts to one per debtor.
Days 8 to 30Using your items: locate debtors from the second contacts, research the business accounts and their owners, and reconcile every balance with you so rent, fees and damages are separate.
Day 30We give you a ready list of accounts where the next step is yours to decide with your attorney: a card retry, a demand letter, retrieving a container, or a suit on the largest balances.
Every monthOne page, plain numbers: contacts made, promises, payments, accounts closed out, and what we still need from you.
Day 90Review together against agreed targets, and decide what stays with us.
Our commitments: no automated contact on an account until a person has reviewed it; no new fees; and one named person you can call.

Methodology

Document review. We reviewed the 302 files MI-BOX uploaded to the client portal: 180 placement spreadsheet rows, 111 invoices, six client summaries and one executed agreement. Documents added by SWRS staff on individual debtor records are not included in these counts. Invoice and document counts are matched to debtors by name.

Data pulled live from the SWRS ADS collection system on October 28, 2026, covering all 86 accounts placed under Client Key 9292. Financial figures reconcile exactly to the Account Summary (DOR–DOA) report: $60,793.68 placed, $370.62 recovered, $77,729.78 open. Activity counts are derived from the complete account note log — 17,030 entries after removal of exact duplicates — together with dial records.

Collection activity is conducted in accordance with the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (15 U.S.C. § 1692 et seq.), Regulation F (12 C.F.R. Part 1006), and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. § 1681 et seq.). Southwest Recovery Services is a licensed and bonded collection agency.
